The blood bank at Sanjeevani Hospital was quiet at seven when Rekha closed her shift log. Her brother Kiran was standing by the donor chairs, holding two cups of cutting chai. They had not spoken since the fight over their father's flat, almost three years ago.
"I heard you work nights now," he said. "I brought tea. I also brought an apology, if you'll take it."
Rekha did not reach for the cup at once. Her shoulders stayed high. "I'm glad you came," she said slowly. "But last time your sorry lasted a week. I need you to be honest about what happened, and I need to see that something is different."
Kiran nodded and set the tea down on the counter. "Sunday lunch, somewhere neutral? You choose."
She picked up the cup. "One lunch. Then we'll see."

qa.q: Where was Kiran waiting when Rekha closed her shift log?
qa.a: He was standing by the donor chairs in the blood bank at Sanjeevani Hospital, holding two cups of cutting chai.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when Kiran offered the tea and the apology?
qa.a: She felt wary and guarded, glad he came but not ready to trust him; her high shoulders and slow reply show she was protecting herself after a sorry that lasted a week.

qa.q: What small step let Rekha welcome Kiran without rushing?
qa.a: She agreed to one lunch in a neutral place and asked for honesty, so she could see whether he had changed before offering more closeness.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the moment when Rekha does not take the cup at once?
qa.a: He may feel nervous and a little hurt, but he seems to understand he must earn her trust again, which is why he lets her choose the place.

grounding: A sibling offers a bridge after a long rift and the protagonist welcomes it cautiously, asking for honesty and setting the pace of closeness.

Dear Hrithik bhaiya,
Your message on my birthday reached me in Pune. Four years of silence, and then: "I miss you, Bidi. Can we try?" I read it on the bus and missed my stop.
I want to answer honestly. Part of me is happy. Part of me is still the one who waited alone outside the lawyer's office while you sided with Baba about the house.
So here is what I can offer. A phone call every second Sunday, for now. I'd like you to tell me, in your own words, what you think went wrong, not only that you're sorry. If the calls go well, maybe I come home for Durga Puja. If they don't, I'll step back again, and that will be my choice, not a punishment.
I kept your message. That should tell you something.
Bidisha

qa.a: Four years of silence.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Bidisha describe on reading the message?
qa.a: Bidisha feels happy and hopeful, yet still hurt and wary from waiting alone outside the lawyer's office; missing the bus stop shows how shaken the message left the writer.

The power went out in Hansa's hostel just as her mother's call came through, so she sat on the stairwell with the phone at two per cent battery.
"I don't have long, Ma," she said. "So I'll say the main thing. I forgive you for the years of shouting. I'm doing it so I can stop carrying it."
Her mother started crying. "Then come home for the—"
"Not yet." Hansa pressed her palm against the cold wall. "If we talk, the shouting stops. The first time it starts, I hang up and we try again next week. And I'm not moving back."
Her roommate Bidisha appeared on the landing with a torch and a charger cable. The screen flickered.
"Did you hear me, Ma?"
"I heard," her mother said quietly. "No shouting."

In the staff room of the city hospital pharmacy, Deepika and Nilesh had a running joke: whoever lost the lunchtime crossword bought the evening tea. They had been close since induction.
Then the chief pharmacist asked Deepika to draw up the Diwali-week roster. Nilesh leaned over her shoulder. "You'll give me the day shift, na? My sister's coming."
Deepika laughed but covered the sheet with her hand. "Put in a request like everyone else. I'm going by the dates they came in."
He went quiet for the rest of lunch. That evening she found him at the tea stall.
"I'm not being cold. If I bend it for you, Rinku and the others will notice, and then we're the pair who get favours."
Nilesh sighed, then grinned. "Fine. But you're buying the tea."

qa.q: What did the chief pharmacist ask Deepika to do?
qa.a: Draw up the Diwali-week roster.

qa.q: What does Deepika covering the sheet with her hand suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels awkward and protective, wanting to keep the friendship warm without letting it bend the roster.

qa.q: Why did Deepika go to find Nilesh at the tea stall?
qa.a: To explain her reason calmly so the quiet lunch did not harden into resentment; clearing it up quickly helped the friendship survive the disagreement.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Deepika's refusal at first?
qa.a: He probably feels hurt and let down, since they are close, until her point about fairness makes sense and he can joke again.

grounding: The protagonist enjoys a close work friendship and keeps fairness and boundaries so the bond survives a disagreement.
